entries.meaning: To put clothes on yourself or on another person. ---
examples: He dresses for the weather, not for the office.
She dressed the twins in matching coats.
I was dressing when the phone rang.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (dress the baby), intransitive (he dresses well)
entries.contrast: About yourself Americans say get dressed, not dress myself: I got dressed in five minutes.

entries.meaning: To take clothes off yourself or off another person. ---
examples: The nurse asked him to undress behind the curtain.
She undressed the sleepy child and put him to bed.
He had already undressed and was half asleep.

entries.meaning: To put on different clothes, or to put different clothes on someone. ---
examples: I need to change before dinner.
She changed into jeans the moment she got home.
He is changing the baby in the back room.
entries.contrast: The final e drops before -ing: changing. You change into clothes, not change on.

entries.meaning: To put on a piece of clothing or equipment. ---
examples: Firefighters don full gear before they go in.
She donned a white coat and walked into the lab.
He was donning his uniform when the alarm sounded.
entries.contrast: The n doubles: don → donned, donning. This verb belongs to writing; in speech people say put on.

entries.meaning: To put clothing or cloth over a part of the body. ---
examples: Cover your shoulders before you go inside.
She covered her head with a thin scarf.
His arms were covered to the wrist.
entries.contrast: You cover something with a scarf, a coat, a blanket.

entries.meaning: To decorate a person or an object, especially with jewelry or ornament. ---
examples: Tiny pearls adorn the collar and the cuffs.
She adorned her hair with fresh flowers.
The robe was adorned with gold thread.
entries.contrast: You adorn something with something else.

entries.meaning: To add belts, jewelry, scarves, or bags to an outfit. ---
examples: She knows how to accessorize.
He accessorized the gray suit with a green tie.
The dress is plain, so it can be accessorized any way you like.
entries.contrast: American spelling takes -ize; British writing often has accessorise.

entries.meaning: To change clothes or appearance so that people do not recognize you. ---
examples: A wig alone will not disguise you.
He disguised himself as a delivery driver.
She was disguised in a long coat and dark glasses.
entries.contrast: The s in the middle is a /z/ sound and the u is silent: dis-GYZ.

entries.meaning: To cover the face, or to hide something from view. ---
examples: A bandana will mask the lower half of your face.
The dancers masked their faces for the last scene.
Every one of the riders was masked.

entries.meaning: To cover the face or head with a thin cloth. ---
examples: Traditional dress veils the hair and the neck.
She veiled her face before entering the shrine.
The window was veiled with pale lace.
entries.contrast: Veil sounds exactly like vale, an old word for a valley.

entries.meaning: To supply someone with the clothes or equipment they need. ---
examples: The school outfits every player with a uniform.
They outfitted the whole crew in orange vests.
The store is outfitting the entire wedding party.
entries.contrast: The t doubles: outfit → outfitted, outfitting.

entries.meaning: To wrap a baby tightly in a cloth or a light blanket. ---
examples: Nurses swaddle newborns to keep them calm.
She swaddled the baby and laid him in the crib.
He is swaddling her for the night.

entries.meaning: To wrap someone in warm clothes, or to tie things together in a bunch. ---
examples: Bundle the kids in their snow gear before they go out.
She bundled the baby in two blankets.
The old sweaters were bundled and carried to the attic.

entries.meaning: To put clothing on for a moment to see whether it fits or looks right. ---
examples: Ask whether you can try the next size up.
She tried three jackets and bought none of them.
He is trying the boots in a wider width.
entries.contrast: The y becomes i: try → tries, tried, but trying keeps the y. In a store Americans add on: try on a coat.

entries.meaning: To wear something noticeable and look pleased about it. ---
examples: He likes to sport a bow tie at weddings.
She sported bright red boots all winter.
The whole team was sporting new warm-up jackets.
entries.contrast: This verb has nothing to do with games; sport meaning a game is only a noun.

entries.meaning: To open something that is buttoned, buckled, or zipped. ---
examples: Do not unfasten your seat belt yet.
He unfastened his collar and loosened his tie.
She had unfastened only two buttons.
entries.contrast: The t is silent here too: un-FAS-uhn.

entries.meaning: To close a shirt, coat, or jacket with its buttons. ---
examples: Button your coat, it is freezing out there.
He buttoned the shirt wrong and had to start over.
She is buttoning her daughter's sweater.
entries.contrast: The final n does not double, because the stress is on the first syllable: buttoned, buttoning.

entries.meaning: To open a shirt or coat by undoing its buttons. ---
examples: He unbuttons his cuffs whenever he works.
She unbuttoned her coat in the warm room.
His shirt was unbuttoned at the neck.

entries.meaning: To close something with a zipper. ---
examples: This jacket zips all the way to the chin.
She zipped her bag and ran for the bus.
He is zipping the kids into their snowsuits.
entries.contrast: The p doubles: zip → zipped, zipping. Americans call the fastener a zipper.

entries.meaning: To open a zipper. ---
examples: Unzip the lining and pull it out.
He unzipped his hoodie and sat down.
The tent had been unzipped from the inside.
entries.contrast: The p doubles: unzip → unzipped, unzipping.

entries.meaning: To fasten a belt, a shoe, or a strap with a buckle. ---
examples: Buckle the strap under his chin.
She buckled her sandals and stood up.
He was buckling the belt on the last notch.

entries.meaning: To undo a buckle. ---
examples: Wait until the plane stops to unbuckle your belt.
He unbuckled his sandals at the door.
She had already unbuckled the child from the car seat.

entries.meaning: To pull laces through the holes of a shoe or boot and tie them. ---
examples: Lace the boots tight before a long hike.
He laced his skates in a hurry.
She knelt on the step, lacing her running shoes.
entries.contrast: The verb lace and lace, the delicate fabric, are spelled and said the same way.

entries.meaning: To fasten something with a knot or a bow. ---
examples: He can tie his own shoes now.
She tied the sash in a neat bow.
The apron was tied so loosely that it came undone.
entries.contrast: The -ing form changes its spelling: tie → tying, never tieing.

entries.meaning: To undo a knot or a bow. ---
examples: Untie the apron and hang it on the hook.
He untied his boots out on the porch.
She was untying the ribbon as carefully as she could.
entries.contrast: Same spelling change as tie: untying, not untieing.

entries.meaning: To tie something into a knot. ---
examples: Knot the ends of the scarf together.
He knotted his tie in front of the mirror.
The laces were knotted so tightly that I had to cut them.
entries.contrast: The k is silent and the t doubles: knot → knotted, knotting. It sounds exactly like not.

entries.meaning: To fasten a necklace, a bracelet, or a bag with its clasp. ---
examples: Can you clasp this necklace for me?
She clasped the bracelet around her wrist.
The purse is clasped with a small brass catch.

entries.meaning: To fasten something with a hook, or to hang it on one. ---
examples: Hook the top of the dress first, then zip it.
She hooked the strap and pulled the zipper up.
His jacket was hooked over the back of the chair.

entries.meaning: To undo something that is fastened with a hook. ---
examples: Unhook the collar if it feels too tight.
He unhooked the coat from the peg by the door.
The belt had been unhooked and left on the chair.

entries.meaning: To hold something in place with a strap. ---
examples: Strap the helmet under your chin.
She strapped the baby into the carrier.
The sandals are strapped around the ankle.
entries.contrast: The p doubles: strap → strapped, strapping.

entries.meaning: To pull a belt or a cord tight around something. ---
examples: Cinch the coat at the waist with a wide belt.
She cinched the dress and it looked like a different dress.
The hood is cinched with a drawstring.
entries.contrast: It ends in -ch, so the third person adds -es: cinches.

entries.meaning: To take off a part that is made to come off. ---
examples: The hood detaches with two snaps.
He detached the liner from his winter coat.
The straps can be detached and washed separately.
entries.contrast: It ends in -ch, so the third person adds -es: detaches.

entries.meaning: To pass something long around or through in the shape of a loop. ---
examples: Loop the belt through every belt loop, not just the front ones.
She looped the scarf twice around her neck.
The cord is looped over the hook behind the door.

entries.meaning: To repair a hole in knitted cloth by sewing back and forth across it. ---
examples: My grandmother could darn a sock in ten minutes.
He darned the elbow of his old sweater.
She sat by the window, darning socks.

entries.meaning: To sew a decorative pattern onto cloth with colored thread. ---
examples: She likes to embroider in the evenings.
They embroidered his initials on the pocket.
The jacket is embroidered with red flowers.

entries.meaning: To make cloth by looping yarn with a single hook. ---
examples: She is teaching me to crochet.
He crocheted a blanket for the baby.
She is crocheting a hat for winter.
entries.contrast: The final t is silent: kroh-SHAY. The past crocheted is said kroh-SHAYD.

entries.meaning: To sew two layers of cloth together with padding between them. ---
examples: They quilt together every Thursday afternoon.
She quilted the lining by hand.
He wore a quilted vest under his coat.

entries.meaning: To come apart into loose threads, or to pull knitted work apart on purpose. ---
examples: Cheap sweaters unravel after one season.
The whole sleeve unraveled from one loose thread.
She is unraveling the old scarf to reuse the yarn.
entries.contrast: American spelling keeps one l: unraveled, unraveling; British writing doubles it.

entries.meaning: To catch cloth on something sharp and pull a thread loose. ---
examples: Rings snag fine knits every time.
She snagged her tights on the corner of the desk.
He kept snagging the sweater on the drawer handle.
entries.contrast: The g doubles: snag → snagged, snagging.

entries.meaning: To fold cloth into regular flat folds and sew them in place. ---
examples: They pleat the fabric before attaching the waistband.
She pleated the skirt by hand.
He wore a pleated shirt with his tuxedo.

entries.meaning: To gather cloth into a strip of soft folds, or to push something out of its neat shape. ---
examples: The wind ruffles her skirt every time she crosses the bridge.
She ruffled the hem with a wide band of lace.
His hair was ruffled and his tie was crooked.

entries.meaning: To make something longer, or to become longer. ---
examples: Can you lengthen the sleeves by an inch?
She lengthened the dress by letting down the hem.
The straps have been lengthened as far as they go.

entries.meaning: To cover the inside of a coat, a bag, or a box with another material. ---
examples: They line the winter coats with flannel.
She lined the jacket with cheap silk.
The boots are lined with wool.
entries.contrast: You line something with a material, and the inner layer itself is the lining.

entries.meaning: To turn the bottom of a sleeve or a pant leg up into a fold. ---
examples: He likes to cuff his jeans above his boots.
She cuffed the sleeves of his big sweater twice.
The pants came back cuffed and pressed.

entries.meaning: To get small folds and creases in cloth, or to put them there. ---
examples: Linen wrinkles if you look at it.
The shirt wrinkled badly in the suitcase.
He showed up in a wrinkled jacket.
entries.contrast: The w is silent: RING-kuhl.

entries.meaning: To press a sharp line into cloth, or to get an unwanted fold in it. ---
examples: Marines crease their trousers razor sharp.
He creased the slacks down the front.
Her dress was badly creased after the flight.

entries.meaning: To open out something that has been folded. ---
examples: Unfold the shirt carefully so it does not wrinkle.
She unfolded the dress and hung it by the window.
The napkin had been unfolded and left on the chair.

entries.meaning: To put two things together, or to wear one item with another. ---
examples: Pair the gray blazer with dark jeans.
She paired the socks as she folded them.
That skirt is usually paired with boots.
entries.русский: подбирать в пару, сочетать, сочетать с
entries.contrast: You pair one thing with another. Pair, pear the fruit, and pare meaning to peel all sound alike.

entries.meaning: To divide things into groups, or to keep them apart. ---
examples: Separate the whites from the darks.
She separated the wool items before washing.
The delicates are separated into a mesh bag.
entries.contrast: The verb ends in /eɪt/, SEP-uh-rayt; the adjective separate is SEP-rit. There is an a in the middle: sep-a-rate.

entries.meaning: To look right together, or to find something that goes with something else. ---
examples: Those shoes do not match the belt.
She matched the scarf to her coat.
They showed up in matching sweaters.
entries.contrast: The third person adds -es: matches. You match one thing to or with another.

entries.meaning: To look bad together, especially two colors or patterns. ---
examples: Orange and pink clash, but she wears them anyway.
The tie clashed with his shirt.
Those two patterns are clashing badly.
entries.contrast: One color clashes with another.

entries.meaning: To go well with something and make it look better. ---
examples: A gray tie would complement that suit.
The blue scarf complemented her eyes.
The pieces were chosen to be complemented by simple jewelry.
entries.contrast: Complement, with an e, means goes well with. Compliment, with an i, means kind words. They sound the same.

entries.meaning: To be clearly different from something beside it, or to set two things side by side to show the difference. ---
examples: White stitching contrasts nicely with black leather.
The designer contrasted heavy wool with thin silk.
A contrasting collar makes a plain shirt look custom.
entries.contrast: The verb is stressed on the second syllable, kuhn-TRAST; the noun is KAHN-trast. One thing contrasts with another.

entries.meaning: To look good on a particular person, or to be right for them. ---
examples: That color really suits you.
The short haircut suited her.
He is not suited to a job with a dress code.
entries.contrast: Suit means it looks good on you; fit means it is the right size. A jacket can fit and still not suit you.

entries.meaning: To arrange clothes or hair to create a particular look. ---
examples: She can style one dress five different ways.
They styled the shoot in 1970s clothes.
His hair was styled for the photograph.

entries.meaning: To hold a position so that someone can photograph or paint you. ---
examples: Pose by the window where the light is better.
They posed in their graduation gowns.
She was posing for the camera in her new coat.

entries.meaning: To show something off openly so that everyone notices it. ---
examples: He likes to flaunt his expensive watches.
She flaunted the new boots all week.
They were flaunting their designer bags on the boardwalk.
entries.contrast: Flaunt, to show off, is not flout, to break a rule openly.

entries.meaning: To make one feature more noticeable than the rest. ---
examples: A belt will accentuate your waist.
The dark trim accentuated his shoulders.
Her height was accentuated by the long coat.

entries.meaning: To hang down loosely because the shape is gone. ---
examples: Cheap knits sag at the knees.
The pockets sagged from all the keys he carried.
His jeans were sagging below his hips.
entries.contrast: The g doubles: sag → sagged, sagging.

entries.meaning: To rub the skin until it is sore. ---
examples: A wet collar will chafe.
The backpack strap chafed her shoulder.
His heels were chafed raw by the new boots.

entries.meaning: To pull at something with a short, sharp movement. ---
examples: Do not tug at the loose thread.
She tugged her skirt down as she stood up.
He kept tugging at his collar all through dinner.
entries.contrast: The g doubles: tug → tugged, tugging. You tug at something.

entries.meaning: To move loosely back and forth in the air. ---
examples: Loose shirts flap in this wind.
His open coat flapped as he ran for the bus.
The laundry was flapping on the line.
entries.contrast: The p doubles: flap → flapped, flapping.

entries.meaning: To add decoration to something plain. ---
examples: They embellish the jackets with beads by hand.
She embellished a plain dress with ribbon.
The collar is embellished with tiny crystals.

entries.meaning: To treat something so that water cannot get through it.
examples: Waterproof your boots before the first snow.
He waterproofed the jacket with a spray.
The seams have been waterproofed at the factory.
